Measured **50–80 ms** warm on three consecutive runs over this repository, against S5's 328–342 ms for the provider-free analysis. `freshness_unverifiable` survives for the two cases a comparison genuinely cannot settle: a sidecar witnessing a compiled lane with no `STATIC.*` on disk, where only a compile could reproduce the witness, and a sidecar protocol tag this build does not read. One effect remains beyond reading files, stated rather than hidden: the ownership question of `#SYS-ARTIFACTS-NOT-TRACKED` is asked by spawning `git ls-files`, only where a `.git` entry exists, and "cannot tell" is reported as unknown rather than as clean — asking git rather than carrying a second ignore engine is the same choice `vibe check`'s own discoverable-block walk made.

p.SYS-SESSION-TARGET: **Decided 2026-11-10 — a gated row is evaluated against an explicitly supplied session target, never against the generator's host.** The condition grammar is closed and already exact: `crates/vibe-core/src/manifest/package/when.rs:71-112` accepts `os:windows` / `os:macos` / `os:linux` and `installed:<group>/<name>` and refuses anything else by name, and the enum has exactly those two variants. `installed:` is a **generation-time** decision owned by `install/bootgen/conditions.rs:86-96` — false drops the contribution entirely, true removes the condition — so only an `os:` gate survives into band G. `prepare` therefore requires an explicit session target when band G is non-empty; an absent or unknown target is **unresolved input**, reported as such, and never resolved to the operating system of whatever machine once generated the prefix. An unknown selector never becomes `true`. The prefix itself stays portable **when the node says so**, which is the default; the owner's decision of 2026-11-10 makes baking an OS an explicit per-project choice rather than the rejected alternative it was when this fact was written — see `#SYS-HOST-AND-TARGET`, which supersedes `#SYS-OWNER-QUESTIONS` Q3 and governs this fact wherever the two differ. Everything above still describes the `host = "portable"` case exactly.

p.SYS-HOST-AND-TARGET: **Owner decision 2026-11-10 — two platform axes, not one, and they are different questions. This supersedes `#SYS-OWNER-QUESTIONS` Q3's "portable, full stop" default.** The manifest's `[system_prompt]` gains two optional keys: `host = "portable" | "linux" | "windows" | "macos"` (default `"portable"`) and `target = ["linux", …]` (default: every operating system). **`host` is where the agent runs; `target` is what the product is for**, and the case that proves they cannot be one key is ordinary: a Linux workstation building Windows software. **`host` governs the existing `when = "os:<name>"` gate**, which has always meant the session's own operating system — a devops, shell or package-manager rule. `"portable"` keeps the behaviour this document already specifies: an `os:` row stays in the gated continuation band and is evaluated per session against an explicitly supplied session target (`#SYS-SESSION-TARGET`). A **fixed** OS resolves those rows at build time and bakes them into the prefix — a matching row is included, a non-matching row is dropped — so a fixed-host prefix has an empty band G and `prepare` needs no session target for it. When a session's own OS then differs from the fixed host, `vibe prompt check` and `vibe prompt prepare` **warn and continue; they do not refuse**: the prefix is a deliberate project declaration, and refusing would make a cross-platform worker unable to read its own project's instructions. **`target` introduces a new gate spelling, `when = "target:<os>"`**, for a rule about the platform the software itself addresses — a kernel interface, WinAPI, a filesystem semantic. Because that is a property of the project and never of a session, it is **always** resolved at build time, whatever `host` says: a `target:` row is included exactly when its OS is in `target`, and an absent `target` selects every OS, so **no existing project's boot changes**. A `target:` row therefore never reaches band G, and the band model of `#SYS-BANDS` is unchanged — only `os:` rows can be gated, and only under `host = "portable"`. **Two consequences worth stating before someone reads them as contradictions.** First, a baked host OS is **not** a violation of `#SYS-NO-VOLATILE`'s ban on "the result of environment detection": nothing is detected. The OS name is read from the node's own authored manifest, exactly like `entrypoint` or `recipe`, so the prefix stays a pure function of its declared inputs and `#SYS-DETERMINISM` holds unchanged — two checkouts of one commit still produce identical bytes, on every host. Detecting the generating machine's OS remains forbidden. Second, two projects that declare different hosts get different prefixes, which is correct: they have different inputs. **Where the work lands.** The `[system_prompt]` keys, their closed value sets and their refusals are **implemented in P1**: an unknown OS refuses naming the field, every legal OS and `portable`; `target = []` refuses, because an empty selection and an absent key mean opposite things and `[]` would silently drop every `target:` row; a repeated OS refuses. The `when = "target:<os>"` grammar itself — a third variant in the closed condition set of `crates/vibe-core/src/manifest/package/when.rs:71-112`, resolved at generation time beside `installed:` in `crates/vibe-workspace/src/install/bootgen/conditions.rs:86-96`, and therefore never a residual `when` in `INDEX.md` — lands in **P2**, where the continuation plan is classified and `conditions.rs` is already being read. Baking `os:` rows under a fixed host landed in **P3** with the composer, and the host-mismatch warning in **P5** with `check` and `prepare` — both delivered 2026-11-10, which completes this fact. **As delivered, three details worth having here rather than only in the format record.** The warning is one shared function, so the two verbs cannot drift apart in what they say; it rides the human report and the `warnings[]` of both `--json` documents, and it never touches an exit status — `check` stays `equal` and `prepare` hands back every band. The session's own operating system is an **injected input** (`CheckRequest::session_os`, filled from the compile-time `std::env::consts::OS`), never a call inside the composer, and it **decides no gate**: `prepare`'s explicitly supplied `--session-target` still selects band G alone, and where that input is given it *is* the session OS the warning is measured against. A session OS this build does not name warns about nothing, for the same reason an unknown session gate never becomes `true`. And `vibe agent` prints the same sentence as a stderr note — not required by this fact, which names `check` and `prepare`, but a launch is the third place a session's own OS is a fact, and the note is kept to the weakest useful form: no flag, no document, never a refusal. `vibe check` deliberately carries none of it, because which machine a contributor is sitting at is not a project defect. The format record is `SP-FMT-101`.

api.title: 8. The API boundary, authority and agent modes

p.SYS-ROLE-PLACEMENT: **Decided 2026-11-10 — a filename chooses no API role, and moving repository text into an instruction role is not semantically neutral.** A supported adapter places the project's trusted instructions explicitly in a supported instruction role (`system`, `developer`, or the equivalent provider field), preserving any mandatory external instructions and the user-set boundaries that already apply. The elevation is acknowledged rather than assumed away: project instructions, package boot text, examples and operational grants do not acquire provider-level authority merely by being on disk or by being in a file called `SYSTEM.md`, and a text separator inside one message creates no real role boundary. The one thing a repository file cannot do is fix an agent that does not let its caller control its own prefix or its auto-loading; such an agent is simply not part of the guaranteed integration, and saying so is more useful than pretending a Markdown file solves it.

p.SYS-NO-DOUBLE-INJECTION: **A supported adapter never injects the prefix and then auto-loads the same entrypoint or lane again.** Supplied sources are accounted for explicitly, which is the only reason the transport contract can say what it says. Double injection is the failure this feature most plausibly produces — it would double the cost it exists to reduce while leaving the agent two copies of the same instructions — so it is a named qualification scenario proved by capturing the actual request against a local fake provider, not an assurance. **Qualified 2026-11-10 (P6, P7).** The entrypoint's text crosses the captured request **exactly once**, counted at a loopback fake provider and again over the envelope document in `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/accept.sh`. P7 adds the cross-delivery form the plan did not ask for: the file Claude Code's slot flag names and the bytes Codex's layered profile file carries are proved equal **to each other** as well as to the reference stream, so a divergence between two adapters is a failure rather than something nobody looked at. A test that compared each adapter to `AGENT-LANE.md` would have compared each to itself.

p.SYS-WORKER-EXCLUSION: **Decided 2026-11-10 — a quiet worker does not receive the central prefix at all, not even briefly.** The profile and the packet are selected **before** the request is constructed, so the central prefix is never assembled for a bounded worker; there is no "ignore the parts that do not apply to you" clause in the prefix and there is deliberately no attempt to write one. A later message cannot return spent context and cannot restore a delegation boundary that has already been crossed. A central session gets the profile of its own selected node; a root's legitimate aggregation of its own subtree stays legitimate (PROP-009 `#MATRYOSHKA-SCOPES`), and the rule is "no content from outside the selected effective scope", not "no members". **Qualified 2026-11-10 (P6, P7).** A node that has not opted in has no prefix to assemble, so `vibe prompt capture` on it refuses naming the opt-in, and the refusal is asserted to carry **none** of the central node's canaries — not the frame's, not the entrypoint's. The scope half is asserted on a workspace member: a member node publishes its own prefix from its own template and carries no byte of the root's frame or entrypoint, while the root's own prefix is untouched by the member's build. The one question an offline test cannot answer — whether a Claude Code subagent inherits the slot — is P9 row C5, and a failure there overrides a passing delivery row because it would mean `launch` must not be that harness's default at all. **Answered 2026-11-10 (P9): row C5 passed.** In a launched session on the live check's sample project, a subagent whose only task was to report whether it could see a lane marker reported no `CANARY-…` word and no `vibe:lane-begin` line — only the managed block's own format example, which the instruction file carries in prose for the router to explain itself. So a Claude Code subagent does **not** inherit `--append-system-prompt-file`, and `launch` stays that harness's default. Measured on Claude Code 2.1.322, Linux, in print mode, one session; the record is `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/live/RESULTS.md`.

p.SYS-NO-HOME-EXPANSION: **Nothing user-local is pulled in by reference.** An authored instruction that *mentions* a home directory, a stewardship settings or plan file, a custody or handoff record, or a token path is an instruction to a tool-using agent, not permission to embed that file's contents; the exporter opens none of them. Package boot text and ordinary repository documents do not acquire instruction authority just because they sit on disk and are reachable. Legitimate user-local observations reach a session through an explicit runtime contract in band T, chosen per request by the caller — which is also what keeps an ostensibly shared prefix from differing by user and from accidentally publishing confidential material. The qualification for this is a sentinel test: the files exist, and they are proved never opened and never present in the output.

p.SYS-CACHE-FACTS: **Checked provider properties, 2026-11-07, recorded as evidence and not as a product contract.** OpenAI: the cache depends on matching the actual rendered prefix, including tools and other request parts; a stable instruction block helps, while retention, eligibility and write conditions depend on the model, and the hit must be read from real usage. Anthropic: the Messages API takes `cache_control` and the hierarchy is tools, then system, then messages, so a change to an early block affects later matches, and entries have a limited lifetime. Gemini: implicit caching exists and a common early prefix is recommended, while explicit caching depends on the API and model and is not universal. Specific prices, TTLs and model lists are deliberately **not** frozen into this document: they change, and a design that encoded them would be wrong within a quarter. A text artifact is not a portable KV cache, does not transfer between models or providers, does not by itself reduce the amount of context a session needs, and does not reconcile contradictory instructions. Stabilising a large prefix is not the same as deserving one: whether the boot a session loads should be that large at all remains a separate engineering question this feature does not answer. **Documented 2026-11-10 (P8), unchanged in substance.** `docs/system-prompt/README.md` §6 carries the provider-owned half as limitations rather than as features: no portable KV cache, equal bytes not proving an identical remote prefix, the tool list ahead of the system slot in every hierarchy checked, a model switch paying the lane again, a resumed session's recorded prompt, a hidden flag and a labelled config option either of which may change, a ~310 KB lane that compaction cannot drop, and user-local instruction files outside vibe's accounting. Every one is marked as not measured where it was not. **One cache read was observed 2026-11-10 (P9), and it is recorded with its scope rather than as a promise.** On a 202,349-byte lane a second Claude Code session in the same project reported `cache_creation_input_tokens` **0** and `cache_read_input_tokens` **85,262**; the same lane bytes at a different checkout path, in a git repository with a dirty tree, reported a **75,803**-token read; and on this repository's own 312,345-byte lane the repeat read was **183,981** tokens. That is the evidence that `--exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections` keeps per-machine text out of the cached prefix — the one thing the flag's help text claims and nothing offline can check. **The scope is part of the observation:** one account, one model (`claude-opus-5-5`), one Claude Code version (2.1.322), every run inside one hour, in print mode, on Linux, with the counters read from each run's own JSON `usage` record. **TTL, cost, latency, hit rate and any saving remain unmeasured**, this changes no product contract, and a text artifact is still not a portable KV cache. Record: `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/live/RESULTS.md`.

p.SYS-CACHE-ECONOMICS: **The economics are parametric, and a saving is claimed only when measured.** For a prefix of L tokens with W cache writes and H cache reads, compare `L × (W + H) × uncached_rate` against `L × (W × write_rate + H × read_rate) + storage_cost` where storage is billed, then add the uncacheable requests and the unchanged cost of the dynamic and output tokens. The numbers come from the current rates and the observed usage, never from this document. A first request and frequent expiries can reduce or erase the benefit entirely. Byte repeatability and the exact request envelope are provable offline against a fake provider; a claim about real money requires a separate measurement of cache write and read tokens, latency and cost on named models, which is **not** performed by this design and is authorised separately (`#SYS-OWNER-QUESTIONS` Q5). Padding a prefix with useless text to reach a provider's minimum cacheable length is forbidden outright. **Documented 2026-11-10 (P8), with the placeholder discipline this fact demands.** `docs/system-prompt/README.md` §8 carries the two expressions verbatim, this repository's measured sizes as the input to **L**, an explicit "substitute current rates", the note that a token count depends on the tokenizer so the provider's own usage report is the measurement, and the two caveats that can erase the benefit — a first request and frequent expiries. No rate, no TTL and no saving appears anywhere in it, and §6 states that none is claimed because measuring one spends real money on named models and is separately authorised.

p.SYS-HARNESS-DELIVERY: **Owner decision 2026-11-10 — three delivery tiers, one mode per harness, and every launch mechanism is file-based. Adopted as decided from `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/HARNESS-DELIVERY.md` (decisions D1–D12 of its §11), which is the design authority for the detail.** The tiers are **launch** (vibe hands the composed agent lane to the harness's own system/developer slot through `vibe agent <harness>`, before the first request), **import** (an `@path` line inside the managed block, which the harness inlines), and **read** (the router block of `#SYS-NO-RECURSION` tells the agent to read the files with its tools). The setting is `[system_prompt.harness.<name>] delivery`, default `launch` for `claude` and `codex` and `read` for every other harness; it decides both the managed block's shape and what `vibe agent` does. **`import` is reserved and refused in version 1**, with a message naming its four blockers: it cannot be chosen per harness while the three entrypoint files are byte-identical (so one import line reaches every import-processing harness and would deliver the lane twice), the lane is not import-inert (`#SYS-IMPORT-INERTNESS`), it is unconditional and so reaches quiet workers in violation of `#SYS-WORKER-EXCLUSION`, and it follows a harness's downward discovery into nested projects. **Ambient config carriers are refused outright** — a project file a harness reads on every launch (`.codex/config.toml`, OpenCode `instructions`, pi `APPEND_SYSTEM.md`) lands in the slot like launch but is unconditional like import, so it too reaches quiet workers. For Codex the carrier is instead a launch-time profile file, and `vibe agent codex` **may** write `$CODEX_HOME/vibe-<node-id>.config.toml` — written only by `vibe agent` and `vibe prompt flags`, never by an install — because the alternative is no launch tier for Codex at all. **No lane bytes ever go on a command line.** A single argument is capped at 128 KiB on Linux (measured: 200,000 bytes refused, 120,000 accepted) and the whole command line at about 32,767 characters on Windows, while the lane is about 310 KB — so the inline route fails on every operating system, not only Windows, and a harness with no file-based slot simply has no launch tier. Three further decisions, each stated so it is not re-argued: the slot carries the **lane only**, not the template, which is written for an API runner with no base prompt and can contradict a harness's own; `vibe agent claude` passes `--exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections`; and `vibe agent` performs **no** OS detection to bake `os:` rows under `host = "portable"`, leaving them to the router, which keeps the artifact a pure function of declared inputs. An entrypoint whose managed block would fall outside Codex's 32 KiB `project_doc_max_bytes` truncation is a **refusal**, and a warning within 4 KB of it. The safe-by-construction property that makes `launch` a defensible default before any live run: a project in `launch` mode started *plain* simply has no markers in context, and the router reads — so the two tiers share one byte-identical block and a project can never contradict itself. Format record: `SP-FMT-105`. **The entrypoint-size half is implemented 2026-11-10 (P2b), and the owner's two severities are one measurement.** `CodexBudget::of(end)` classifies the managed block's end offset as `Fits` / `Near` / `Truncated` against `PROJECT_DOC_MAX_BYTES` (32 KiB) and `PROJECT_DOC_WARN_MARGIN` (4 KB); the write path raises `Truncated` as a refusal **before any write**, and the `Near` warning is `vibe check`'s, because `write_boot_artifacts` has no warning channel and a warning nothing can report is not a warning. `HARNESS-DELIVERY.md` §8.5 had placed that warning in `vibe prompt check`; it is earlier and elsewhere for that reason, and it reads the limit from the write path's own constants rather than carrying a second copy of a ceiling. The delivery table itself, its defaults and the constraints C1–C4 remain P5's. **Qualified offline 2026-11-10 (P7) for the two tiers that ship, and documented (P8).** The three tiers' per-harness matrix, the refusal of `import` with its four blockers, the refusal of ambient carriers, and the file-based rule are `docs/system-prompt/README.md` §5 and §6, with every non-Claude, non-Codex row marked **research, not measured here**. The launch tier is proved against shims that record their argv and against a reference stream: both adapters deliver the classic boot and the same bytes. Codex's placement is proved against the real harness offline — `codex debug prompt-input` on codex-cli 0.167.0 puts a 312,345-byte lane byte-equal and exactly once at item 2 part 0, head and tail markers each once. **Measured live 2026-11-10 (P9), Claude Code only, exactly as D13 authorised it** — Claude Code 2.1.322, model `claude-opus-5-5`, Linux, through the owner's own `claude2` launcher. **One deviation:** every session ran in **print mode** (`vibe agent claude2 -p "…" --output-format json`), because an agent cannot drive the interactive terminal UI; print mode passes the same slot flag, and the interactive UI is therefore unmeasured. **The launch tier delivers.** A 2,570-byte lane, a 202,349-byte padded one and this repository's own 312,345-byte lane each arrived with the last `vibe:lane-end` line quoted **byte-equal**, all four lane canaries present including the tail, the template's canary **absent**, and **no lane file read with a tool** — so no size limit was found up to 312,345 bytes and the router's presence rule held at the real size. **Classic mode is intact:** with the template and the `[system_prompt]` table removed, a plain harness read `STATIC.md`, `INDEX.md`, `00-core.md` and `90-user.md` in that order, **once each**. **One defect was found and fixed (`6323e8a36`).** `vibe agent <launcher>` **refused** in a project that has not opted in, because it shared `vibe prompt flags`' refusal; a launcher must work in every project, so with no template and therefore no lane the launch now passes no slot flag, prints one note and starts the harness unchanged, and the slot-flag conflict check moves behind that branch because a user's own flag then conflicts with nothing. `vibe prompt flags` keeps its refusal: there is nothing to print. A repeated `--append-system-prompt-file` **keeps the last** and drops the first with no notice, which closes `HARNESS-DELIVERY.md` §13's incomplete claim. **Constraints C1, C2 and C4 are implemented 2026-11-10, each with the content it actually has in a version that cannot represent `import`, and that distinction is the whole of this clause.** `import` is refused at **deserialisation**, so C1, C3 and C4 — all three written as conditions on it — have no declarable antecedent. That is not the same as vacuous, and treating it as such would have left two reachable rules unwritten. **C1 has two halves.** The *shape* half — every declared tier must need the same managed block, because the three instruction files are kept byte-identical and one block's bytes reach every harness — is `system_prompt::one_block_shape`, which is **total** today; it is proved total by a test over every `HarnessDelivery` variant, so the day `import` parses that test fails rather than the rule going quietly unenforced, and a mixed `launch`/`read` declaration is asserted *admissible* because both tiers share the one router block. The *premise* half is reachable now and is C1's own "unless byte-identity is given up": instruction files carrying **different** managed blocks make a per-harness `delivery` a statement about nothing, and `vibe prompt check` says so naming the files. **C4** is §4.1's "several instruction files read by one harness" row, where identical copies are explicitly admitted — "two identical routers, same verdict", duplicated bytes a stated cost — so the finding fires only on divergence, when a harness that reads several of those names (Gemini CLI, Qwen Code) would read two contradicting routers. Its nested-discovery half is `vibe check`'s existing `redirect_block` warning and is **named rather than scanned a second time**, because two walks of one question are two answers to it. **C3** needed nothing: the lane's import-inertness is already the `@`-token census in the same report. **C2** is `vibe agent`'s and not a report's, and implementing it fixed a real defect of the same shape as P9's: a `read`-delivery harness now takes no slot flag, writes no Codex carrier, is **not** gated on the harness's version — gating a carrier that is not delivered is how a launch comes to be refused over a delivery it was never going to perform — and does not refuse a slot flag of the user's own, which conflicts with nothing when vibe passes none. `vibe prompt flags` answers from the same one code path and therefore needs no generated lane for such a harness either. Both halves of each constraint carry a positive and a refusal test; `cli_agent_launch.rs`'s four `c2_*` cases are the launch side, `system_prompt::constraints` the configuration side, and `cli_prompt.rs` the command surface. **What keeps this fact `impl/work`:** §10's row C8 — Windows — did not run, for want of a Windows host, so the delivery measurement is a Linux one; the interactive terminal UI was not measured; and Codex, Qwen Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, pi and dsh were never authorised for a live run, so their rows stay research and their delivery default stays `read`. Runbook: `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/live/RUNBOOK.md`; record: `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/live/RESULTS.md`.

p.SYS-CODEX-DECLARED-BUDGET: **Owner decision 2026-11-10 — "everything must work in Codex", including an instruction file larger than 32 KiB. This amends D11, whose 32 KiB was a constant and is now a default.** The 32 KiB of `#SYS-HARNESS-DELIVERY` is Codex's *own default* `project_doc_max_bytes`, not a law: a user's `~/.codex/config.toml` or a trusted project's `.codex/config.toml` may raise it, so measuring a project against a constant meant refusing a file the Codex that project actually runs would have read whole. The project therefore **declares** the limit it is built for, as `[system_prompt.harness.codex] doc_max_bytes` — a positive integer, validated at deserialisation, with `0` and a negative value refused by name rather than defaulted, and an unknown harness name refused too, because a setting silently ignored is the one failure a configuration table must not have. Absent means Codex's default, so no existing project's behaviour changes. **Both severities read the declaration**, which is what keeps them one measurement rather than two ceilings: the write path's refusal and `vibe check`'s near-limit warning are the same `CodexBudget` against the same number. **Two warnings join `vibe check`.** A declared limit above the default is only real if the Codex that runs has been told, and a Codex started directly rather than through `vibe agent codex` has not been — so the warning hands over the exact one-line setting (`project_doc_max_bytes = <N>` in `~/.codex/config.toml` or a trusted project's `.codex/config.toml`) rather than describing the problem. And the **whole file** is measured as well as the block: what a truncation costs is authored text at the tail, counted in bytes, with the remedy being the boot lane — read as files, truncated by no harness — rather than a shorter instruction file. **P5 carries the launch half:** `vibe agent codex` passes `-c project_doc_max_bytes=<declared>` on every launch, which is short argv and needs no file. **Delivered 2026-11-10 (P5)** and asserted against a shim that records its argv. **But the file the flag accompanies does not work on the Codex that is installed, and that is a falsification of `#SYS-HARNESS-DELIVERY` rather than of this fact.** Probed offline on codex-cli 0.167.0 with `codex debug prompt-input`: `developer_instructions` arrives from the **top level** of `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` and from `-c`, and does **not** arrive from `[profiles.<name>]` either in `config.toml` or in `$CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml` with `-p <name>` — while `-p` is otherwise honoured, so it is that key that is not per-profile in this version. An unknown profile exits 0 silently. The doc-limit flag is therefore correct and live; the lane it accompanies is not delivered. Owner decision, recorded in `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/LOG.md`. **Verified offline against the real harness, 2026-11-10,** with `codex debug prompt-input` (codex-cli 0.167.0), which renders the model-visible prompt input and calls no model: a 43,271-byte `AGENTS.md` carrying the block at the top renders the router whole and drops its tail canary under the default limit, and renders both canaries under `-c project_doc_max_bytes=262144`. Format record: `SP-FMT-107`.

p.SYS-BLOCK-AT-THE-TOP: **Owner decision 2026-11-10 — the managed `<vibevm>` block sits at the **top** of each instruction file, immediately at the start and before any authored text. This is the half of "everything must work in Codex" that needs no configuration.** Every harness that truncates a project instruction file truncates its **tail** — Codex silently, at `project_doc_max_bytes` (`HARNESS-DELIVERY.md` §5, measured against a 40 KB file whose tail canary simply vanished). With the block at the end, the one thing a truncation destroyed was the boot router, and a session then had no idea the project had any boot rules at all; spike S1 had measured exactly that position on this repository, the block occupying offsets 25,291..26,121 of a 26,121-byte `AGENTS.md` — its tail. With the block first, a truncation costs authored prose, which is legible to its author and reportable, and the router always arrives. **Migration happens exactly once.** A block already at offset zero is spliced in place as before; a block anywhere else is moved to the top, the authored text on either side keeping its own order and its own characters, and a second write then finds the block at offset zero and changes nothing. The **one** normalisation is the run of newlines that *separated* the block from the authored text: vibe wrote that separator when it appended the block, so it travels with the block rather than being left behind as a stray blank line — stated plainly because "authored text preserved byte for byte" is otherwise not quite true of it. Measured on this repository's own regeneration: the authored text of all three files is byte-identical and in the same order, with one blank line removed at the old seam and one added at the new one. **The consequence for the budget**, which is why the two decisions of this day belong together: the block's own end is no longer the interesting measurement — at roughly 2 KB it effectively always fits, and D11's refusal survives as a guard reachable only by declaring a limit smaller than the block itself. What a truncation now costs is authored text, and that is the measurement `#SYS-CODEX-DECLARED-BUDGET` added. Format record: `SP-FMT-108`.

p.SYS-NO-RECURSION: **Owner requirement 2026-11-10 — no recursion and no inconsistency across harnesses, including the ones that put the instruction file into the system prompt. This supersedes the earlier sketch in which agent mode imported `SYSTEM.md`.** **Agent mode never delivers `SYSTEM.md`.** `SYSTEM.md` contains the entrypoint, and a harness has already loaded the entrypoint, so importing the prefix *from* the entrypoint is entrypoint → prefix → entrypoint recursion and double delivery with two contradicting managed blocks. Agent mode delivers the **lane** (`#SYS-AGENT-LANE`); `SYSTEM.md` stays the API artifact. **Composition proves the other direction closed:** the prefix's entrypoint segment replaces the managed block with fixed text that contains **no `@` import line and no router**, and the composer *verifies* the composed bytes contain neither — so even a mistaken import of `SYSTEM.md` cannot recurse. **The router scopes itself.** It governs only the project whose root holds the file it sits in; a managed block a harness concatenated in from a sub-directory or a dependency copy is not this session's boot and is ignored, and a task carrying the subagent quiet clause ignores the block entirely. `vibe` **neutralises** the managed block in the copies it materialises under `vibedeps/`, and `vibe check` warns about a nested managed block reachable by a harness's downward discovery. **Several instruction files are mutually consistent by construction.** Gemini CLI and Qwen Code (a Gemini CLI fork) both process `@path` imports recursively, both discover context files in parent *and* sub-directories and concatenate them, and both can be configured to read several names (`AGENTS.md` plus `QWEN.md`). So the router's test is "the lane is present **anywhere** in your context", never "above": concatenation order, and which of two files carries the router, cannot change the outcome. Duplicated bytes are a stated cost, never a contradiction. Verified repository facts behind this: **18** tracked instruction files carry a `<vibevm>` managed block — this fact read 19, and the count was corrected in P2b by a census over `git ls-files`: six directories × three names, while `vibevm/vibepacks/org.vibevm.fractality/CLAUDE.md` and one staging fixture mention `<vibevm>` in prose and carry no marker pair — and tracked `GEMINI.md` files exist under `research/rust-demo`, `research/ts-demo`, `vibevm/vibedeps/org.vibevm.fractality.delegation-rules/1.0.0` and `vibevm/vibepacks/org.vibevm.fractality/{delegation-rules,fractality}/v1.0.0`. Design document: `HARNESS-DELIVERY.md` §3 and §4. **Implemented 2026-11-10 (P3) for composition's half, with the scope of the `@` check stated exactly, because the literal reading is unsatisfiable on this very repository.** The composer proves two things over the whole composed prefix — no exactly standalone `<vibevm>` or `</vibevm>` line, and no lane marker line — which together are the mechanical form of "the managed block was replaced and no router survived", and both refuse by line number. The *no `@` import line* half is proved over the **bytes the composer itself wrote**: the frame lines and the transport contract. It cannot be proved over the whole artifact, because the compiled lane of this repository carries 68 `@spec://` reference tokens that `#SYS-LANE-VERBATIM` forbids rewriting and `#SYS-TEMPLATE-LITERAL` forbids treating a user's own character as a directive — so what the composer carries is **reported** (`#SYS-IMPORT-INERTNESS`) and what the composer authored is **refused**. Stated plainly so the gap is not mistaken for an oversight: a harness that resolves `@` references inside imported content would still act on those carried tokens, and that is precisely why the `import` tier is refused rather than why this check is weaker than it looks. **Implemented 2026-11-10 (P2b) for the block's half — the generator's three remaining obligations under this fact — with four things made exact.** The router's body is one function, `boot_artifacts::redirect::router::render_router`, over a three-member `RouterFacts { node_id, static_hash12, spec_format }`, pinned byte for byte by a golden test: that golden and that function are the whole review surface for a diff that touches every instruction file in every project. The facts travel as a **value** rather than as a derivation each side repeats — the write seam computes them once per generation and capture takes the same value — because the first test run showed the two sides disagreeing about the node id, which is the drift `#SYS-PROSPECTIVE-ENTRYPOINT` exists to prevent. The node id is `Manifest::consumer_node().coordinate()`, with the workspace's own coordinate and then the reserved spelling `-` behind it, because `write_boot_artifacts` is reachable for a bare directory that is no workspace's node and refusing to publish a boot lane there over an identity the lane does not depend on would be the wrong trade; `-` is a token no manifest can produce, so the scope test still fails closed. **Neutralisation is a function, not a sentence**: `vibedeps::instruction_block::for_file` replaces the block body in every copy the three materialisation walks place, leaves every byte outside the markers to the package that published it, and copies verbatim a file that is not UTF-8 or whose markers are not exactly one ordered pair — repairing someone else's malformed pair is the repair `locate_block` refuses on our own. `vibe check`'s nested-block warning and its un-neutralised-copy warning went into the existing `redirect_block` cell rather than a new check id, and reproduced the 18-file census independently as 15 findings. **Regenerated 2026-11-10 (P4), and the count needs one correction of its own.** `vibe reinstall` over the materialised tree — no fetch, no network, nothing inside the markers hand-edited — rewrote the **three** instruction files of this repository's one node, at the new top-of-file position of `#SYS-BLOCK-AT-THE-TOP`. The other fifteen of the eighteen are not this project's to rewrite: six belong to the nested projects under `research/`, nine to packages under `vibevm/vibepacks/` and `vibevm/vibedeps/`, and each is its own project's regeneration — which is precisely what the router's self-scoping is for, and what `vibe check`'s nested-block and un-neutralised-copy warnings report. The P2b blocker is recorded for the next worker: the real user cache disagreeing with the lockfile pin is routed around by running the generator under an isolated `HOME` / `VIBE_SETTINGS` / `VIBE_REGISTRY_CACHE`, and `vibe reinstall` — which recomputes boot artifacts from the tree already on disk and never re-resolves — is the narrower command than `vibe install`.

p.SYS-IMPORT-INERTNESS: **Owner requirement 2026-11-10 — imported content must be inert for the harness that imports it, and today the lane is not.** `STATIC.xml` carries 68 tokens of the form `@spec://…`, and five of the eight INDEX files carry `@` tokens too. Gemini CLI and Qwen Code process `@path` recursively inside imported content, and Claude Code does so to a depth limit, so an imported lane could make a harness try to resolve a `spec://` address as a file path. `vibe` composes the lane **verbatim** (`#SYS-LANE-VERBATIM`) and therefore may not rewrite those tokens. Two consequences. `import` stays refused until either boot text stops emitting such tokens or a live run shows a given harness leaves them alone — and the test is **per harness and per flavour**: before choosing an import flavour `vibe` verifies there is no triggering token outside a code fence, and otherwise falls back to router-only delivery, where the file is read through the agent's file tool and no import processing happens at all. `vibe prompt check` reports the token count and the first few locations. **Implemented 2026-11-10 (P3) as a census, and the unit is a token rather than a line — which matters, because counting lines understates this repository's lane by sixteen.** A site is an `@` that opens a reference token (its preceding byte is not itself a token byte, and at least one token byte follows), recorded with its segment, line, column, the token itself, whether it starts its line, and whether it sits inside a code fence. Measured on this tree: **68** tokens in `STATIC.xml`, every one outside a fence — which independently confirms the number this fact was written with — of which 52 start their line; and **74** in the whole composed agent lane, the extra six coming from the INDEX files. The census travels with each composed artifact; the refusal of an import flavour and the `vibe prompt check` report are P5's, made from this evidence. **One live observation 2026-11-10 (P9), and it is narrow on purpose.** Asked, in a launched Claude Code session carrying this repository's whole 312,345-byte lane, to report the `@spec://` tokens it could see, the agent reported them **without having tried to resolve any of them as a path** — the repository leg of row C1 reports no such attempt (`campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/live/RESULTS.md`). That is one harness, one version (2.1.322), one session, and it is evidence about the **launch** tier, where the lane arrives as slot text and no import processing runs at all. It does **not** make the lane import-inert and it does not reopen `import`: the test is per harness and per flavour, Gemini CLI and Qwen Code — the two that resolve `@path` recursively inside imported content — were never run, and the 74 tokens are still there.

p.SYS-BOOT-ORDER-IS-PRECEDENCE: **Owner decision 2026-11-10 (D12) — the boot order is an order of precedence, not of position, and PROP-009 gains one sentence saying so.** PROP-009 `#SESSION-START-ORDER` reads as a sequence in time: the entrypoint, then `STATIC`, then the INDEX entries. In launch delivery the lane arrives **first**, and in a stronger role. Rather than leave the published contract quietly false, the rule is restated: a conforming delivery may place the lane before the entrypoint, and a lane delivered earlier counts as read. Two honest consequences. Lane text gains instruction-role authority it does not have as a tool result, which `#SYS-ROLE-PLACEMENT` already requires be acknowledged rather than assumed away. And authored text that refers to *position* — "above", "below", "you have just read" — breaks silently; `vibe prompt check` lists such phrases in the entrypoint and the lane for a human to review, and never edits them (`#SYS-NO-REWRITE-OF-AUTHORED-TEXT`). **Half-implemented 2026-11-10 (P2b):** the generated router block now says it in the one place every session reads — its closing paragraph states that the boot order is an order of precedence and that a lane delivered before the file has been read — and a test asserts that no positional word occurs anywhere in the rendered body. **Completed 2026-11-10:** PROP-009 `#SESSION-START-ORDER` now carries D12's sentence — the order is one of precedence, not of position, and a lane already delivered counts as read — so the published contract and the generated router block say the same thing. This fact is `impl/done`.

p.SYS-HARNESS-EXECUTABLE: **Owner decision 2026-11-10, revised the same day — a launcher is a named thing with a kind, and only a user may name one. This amends `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/HARNESS-DELIVERY.md` §8.4, which named the programs directly.** The harness *kind* and the program that runs are two different things, and conflating them was the mistake. A **kind** — `claude`, `codex`, …, a closed set — is the flag dialect and the delivery rules: which slot, which flags, which refusals. A **launcher** is a name bound to a kind and to the argv that starts it. The motivating case is ordinary: a developer reaches a harness through a small personal wrapper that sets the harness's own config directory, drops API-key environment variables and `exec`s the real program with standing flags, passing every argument through. **The shape, in the user configuration only.** `[agent.launchers.<name>]` with `kind` (required, the closed set), `command` (the argv **prefix** to exec — a prefix rather than a path, so a wrapper may carry its own arguments) and an optional `config_dir`. `vibe agent <launcher-name> [args…]` resolves the launcher **by name**, takes its flags and delivery from its kind, and execs `command` + flags + the user's own arguments. The built-in launchers `claude` and `codex` always exist, each with `kind` equal to its name and `command` the program of that name; a user launcher of the same name **overrides** the built-in, which is how a wrapper takes over the plain name without the user retyping it. Any number of launchers may share a kind — two Claude Code launchers with different `config_dir`s are an ordinary configuration, not an edge case — and `vibe agent list` prints each one's name, kind, command, config directory and **source**, built-in or the exact user-config path, because a developer debugging which program ran needs to know which file decided it. An unknown launcher name is a refusal that **lists the available launchers**; an unknown kind is a refusal naming the field. `vibe prompt flags` accepts either a kind or a launcher name. **A project manifest that names a launcher is a refusal.** A repository must not choose which program runs on a contributor's machine: that is the one setting where a shared file would let one developer's convenience execute arbitrary code on everyone else's computer, and it is not a judgement call. **`config_dir` exists for one honest reason:** it names where that launcher's harness keeps its session logs, which the cache diagnostics of `#SYS-CACHE-FACTS` read. A wrapper that sets `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` internally makes the directory unknowable from outside — vibe sees neither the variable nor the harness's default — so a launcher may state it; absent that, vibe takes it from the environment, and absent that, the kind's documented default. **When it is still unknown the diagnostics say so**, rather than guessing a path and reading someone else's logs. Finally, `vibe prompt flags` prints **flags only and never a program**, which is what lets its output be appended to any wrapper, alias or launcher a developer already has. Offline tests: resolution by name; a user launcher overriding a built-in; an argv-prefix exec proved against a shim on `PATH` that records the argv it received; the unknown-name and unknown-kind refusals; the refusal of the table in a project manifest; and `vibe agent list`'s output. **Implemented 2026-11-10 (P5), with one spelling this decision could not have as written.** In the **user** configuration the table is `[launchers.<name>]`, not `[agent.launchers.<name>]`: that file is `~/.vibe/agents.toml`, whose `[agent.<name>]` tables are already PROP-064 agent definitions, so `[agent.launchers]` would be an agent called "launchers". It is the same path with the file's own root elided. `[agent.launchers.*]` keeps its meaning as the spelling a **project manifest** is refused for, quoted verbatim in that refusal — which is asked **before** the workspace opens, because the manifest parser already rejects `[agent]` as an unknown field and "unknown field `agent`" is not the sentence a contributor needs to read. Also implemented: resolution by name with a user launcher overriding a built-in; the argv-prefix exec, by `execve` on a POSIX host so the harness owns the terminal, the signals and the exit status, and by spawn-wait-exit on Windows; the refusal of a user argument that would put a second system prompt in the slot; the lane recomposed at every launch; and `vibe agent list`'s rows with each launcher's source. Proved offline against shims on `PATH` that record their argv: no real harness is ever started and no model is ever called. Format record: `SP-FMT-109`. *(The first form of this decision, superseded within the day and never implemented, put the override on the kind itself as `[agent.<harness>] command` with a `--command` flag and a `VIBE_AGENT_<HARNESS>_COMMAND` variable above it. It could not express two launchers of one kind, which is the case that matters, and a per-run flag plus an environment variable is three precedence tiers where a name needs none.)* **Two behaviours added 2026-11-10 (P9) by the live check, both in `6323e8a36`.** **A project that has not opted in is not a refusal.** There is no template and therefore no lane, so `vibe agent <launcher>` composes nothing, passes no slot flag, prints one note saying the project has not opted in and that the harness starts unchanged, and execs `command` plus the user's own arguments — which is precisely the classic boot the router already handles, and which is why the slot-flag conflict check moved behind that branch: without a lane a user's own slot flag conflicts with nothing. `vibe prompt flags` keeps its refusal, because there is nothing to print. The earlier behaviour — sharing that refusal — made a launcher unusable in every project that had not opted in, which is the opposite of what a launcher is for. **A resume says what it keeps.** When the user's own arguments resume a Claude Code session (`-c`, `--continue`, `-r`, `--resume`, `--resume=<id>`), `vibe agent` prints that the session keeps the boot lane it started with and that boot files edited since reach the agent only in a **new** session. That is row C7 measured, not inferred: a resumed session came back carrying the old band-U file's id, and the router could not notice, because the block states only the static lane's expected id and that file had not changed. Both behaviours are asserted offline against the argv-recording shim, so no harness is started and no model is called. **One Windows defect, found in the row C8 live check (Windows 11, vibe 1.0.12) and fixed 2026-11-10:** `vibe agent claude` answered "starting `claude`: program not found" although Claude Code was installed and on `PATH`, because npm installs it as `claude.cmd` while `Command::new("claude")` finds only `claude.exe` — so a bare `command` word is now resolved on `PATH` through `PATHEXT` (`.COM;.EXE;.BAT;.CMD` when the variable names none, the extension's own case and its lower case, `.ps1` never started because Windows cannot start one without choosing a host, an explicit path used as written) and the **resolved file** is spawned, which keeps the standard library's own `.bat` / `.cmd` argument escaping (CVE-2024-24576) rather than hand-building a `cmd /c` line; the refusal keeps the words "program not found" and now names the search that failed. The same resolution serves the Codex `--version` probe, which would otherwise report unreachable for exactly the `codex.cmd` the launch goes on to start, and it is proved by unit tests over an injected `PATH` and `PATHEXT` that run on every platform.

p.SYS-CODEX-PROFILE-TOP-LEVEL: **Owner directive 2026-11-10 — "everything must work in Codex", and it does: the carrier is `developer_instructions` at the **top level** of the launch-time profile file. This amends D3/D4 of `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/HARNESS-DELIVERY.md` §11 and demotes the **[V]** of its §5 to a version-scoped observation.** P5 recorded the profile carrier as **falsified** on codex-cli 0.167.0 and left the Codex launch tier with no working mechanism. The falsification was of the wrong spelling, not of the carrier. `-p <name>` **layers** `$CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml` *on top of the base user config* — codex-cli's own words for the flag, and its refusal of the legacy `profile = "<name>"` key says the same thing — so the file is read as a configuration file and the key belongs at its top level. Written inside a `[profiles.<name>]` table it is an ordinary nested table that codex-cli loads and never reads. Measured offline with `codex debug prompt-input`, which renders the model-visible prompt and calls no model, in an isolated `CODEX_HOME`: a 314,270-byte value arrives **byte-equal, exactly once**, as the first part of the second developer item, directly behind Codex's base instructions and ahead of skills, permissions, collaboration mode and everything dynamic — the position `#SYS-HARNESS-DELIVERY` assumed. A byte-exact diff of the render with and without the layer differs in exactly the lane's own part and its two provenance keys, so **nothing of the user's configuration and nothing of Codex's base instructions is lost**: layering, not replacing, is why this carrier beats every alternative considered. The rejected candidates and the reason each lost: a launch-scoped overlay `CODEX_HOME` (would have to reproduce a home holding SQLite databases, lock files and live session state — symlinking a database file splits its `-wal`/`-shm` siblings, copying `auth.json` desynchronises token refresh, and unprivileged symlinks do not exist on Windows); `model_instructions_file` with Codex's own base instructions prepended (it **replaces** the base instructions, so correctness would depend on a cached copy of another program's prompt staying correct across its upgrades); and any inline `-c developer_instructions=…` (128 KiB per argument on Linux against a 312 KB lane). **The version is part of the claim.** The carrier is a configuration key, and a key the program does not read produces no warning, no error and no non-zero exit — a session that starts looking exactly right with no boot lane in it, which is the one failure a launch tier must never reach quietly. So `vibe agent <codex launcher>` and `vibe prompt flags --harness codex` ask the launcher's own program its version and **refuse** one this build has not verified, naming the installed version, the verified version (`0.167.0`), the offline command that re-checks it and the field that records a user's own measurement; a version that cannot be read at all is a note rather than a refusal, because "cannot tell" is not "wrong". `[launchers.<name>] harness_version` names a version rather than carrying a boolean, so overriding the gate is an attributable measurement and not a switch. Format record: `SP-FMT-109`, amended.

p.SYS-SOFT-LAUNCH: **Owner directive 2026-11-11 — «сделай чтобы все агенты запускались мягко»: every agent kind launches softly.** `vibe agent <launcher>` must never fail to start the harness because *vibe* could not deliver the lane. A launcher's job is to start a program; the delivery is vibe's side of the bargain, and a developer left with no session because vibe could not keep its own half is the worst of the available outcomes — worse than a session that boots the classic way, which every project already supports, because the managed block's router reads the boot files when it finds no markers (`#SYS-NO-RECURSION`). So whenever safe delivery is impossible the harness starts with **no slot flag and no carrier**, behind **one loud stderr warning** naming the reason and the exact fix command. The causes, each measured as the same outcome: the prefix build failed; the lane file is absent after that build; the lane is **stale** after it, which means the bytes on disk are not this node's current lane; the directory is not a vibe project at all; a Codex version is unverified or its stated `harness_version` is not a version number; and, generally, **any kind's carrier precondition fails** — the rule is written over the precondition rather than over Codex, so a kind added later inherits it. **A stale or half-written lane is never delivered.** If the build failed, the file that happens to be on disk is the previous build's or half of this one's, and putting it in the slot would hand the agent bytes that are not this project's boot lane — strictly worse than handing it none, because the router cannot notice a lane it was given. **`--quiet` does not suppress the warning**, and that is the whole reason it is a warning rather than a note: `--quiet` asks for less narration about what vibe did, while this sentence is about what the **agent receives** — a session without its boot lane, which the developer is about to spend tokens in. Hiding it would make the two launches indistinguishable at the terminal, and the failure mode of the carriers this guards is already silence. **Three refusals remain, and each is about something other than delivery.** A project manifest naming a launcher is security, not delivery (`#SYS-HARNESS-EXECUTABLE`): a repository must not choose which program runs on a contributor's machine, and a soft launch there would start the program the repository chose. An unknown launcher name, and a malformed `agents.toml` under it, leave vibe not knowing *which program to run*, so there is nothing to start softly. And a slot flag of the user's own is refused **only while vibe is itself delivering** — the C2 branch of `HARNESS-DELIVERY.md` §4 — because in every soft, opted-out or `read`-delivery launch vibe passes none and the user's flag conflicts with nothing. **`vibe prompt flags` keeps refusing.** It prints flags and starts nothing, so there is no session to save: flags pointing at a lane that is not there, or at a carrier this harness may not read, are the one answer a shell alias turns silently into a session with no lane in it. The one exception it keeps is the **stale** lane, which it prints beside a note saying so — the flags then point at real bytes and a human reading them can decide, where a launch cannot. That split is why the composition returns the reason as a **value** rather than raising it: one cell deciding both answers would have to know which caller it is in, and the two callers want opposite things from the same facts. **Implemented 2026-11-11.** `commands::prompt::flags::{Composed, Undeliverable}` carry the reason, the fix and whether printing may proceed; `harness_version::gate` returns a verdict instead of raising one; `commands::agent::launch::soft` prints the warning and execs the launcher's own argv with the user's arguments and nothing of vibe's. Proved offline against the argv-recording shims of `cli_agent_launch.rs`: the unverified-Codex case, which was a refusal until this directive, now launches bare and warns; a failed build launches bare while the previous lane is still on disk, asserted not passed; the warning survives `--quiet`; and a directory that is not a project launches bare. No harness is started and no model is called. Format record: `SP-FMT-111`.

p.SYS-OPENCODE: **Owner directive 2026-11-11 — «сделай поддержку opencode»: OpenCode is a harness kind, and its delivery tier is `read` because its carrier cannot be scoped to one launch.** The kind exists — `HarnessKind` is closed at **three** — so `vibe agent opencode` is a built-in launcher, `[system_prompt.harness.opencode] delivery` is declarable rather than an unknown field, `vibe prompt flags --harness opencode` answers, and a Windows `opencode.cmd` resolves through the same `PATHEXT` search `#SYS-HARNESS-EXECUTABLE` added for `claude.cmd`. **Membership is not a launch tier**, and that distinction is the whole of this fact: a kind is here when vibe knows its dialect well enough to answer *what does a launch of this pass*, and OpenCode's answer is "nothing, and here is why". **The carrier was found, measured and then declined.** `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` is an environment variable holding one JSONC configuration document whose `instructions` array is *set-unioned* with the project's own rather than replacing it, writes nothing to disk, and names **file paths** — so the lane never leaves the file it is in and no lane byte goes on a command line or into the environment. Measured offline on OpenCode **2.2.7** against a loopback OpenAI-compatible provider that recorded the request body: the sample project's 204,429-byte lane arrived **byte-equal and exactly once** inside a single system message of 215,504 bytes, all four lane canaries present including the tail, the template's canary absent — and the **control run** with the variable unset produced a 10,928-byte system prompt with no lane and no lane canary, which is what makes "the carrier delivered it" a measurement rather than a coincidence. **One research claim was wrong and the correction is in our favour:** `HARNESS-DELIVERY.md` §5 had `<env>` with today's date *preceding* the instructions, so the lane's cache entry would die at midnight. It does not. In the captured request the instructions begin at offset 7,974 and the lane at 10,312, while `<env>` is at 214,848 and `Today's date` at 214,743 — the per-day text is a **suffix** of a 215 KB prompt, so the lane's bytes are stable across a date change. **Two blockers close the tier, and the first is observed.** *One:* OpenCode's default mode serves every session from one long-lived background service on a fixed port, and that process has the environment of whoever started it — with the variable set in the client's environment, `opencode debug config` against the running service lists the global config and **no such layer**, while the same command under `--standalone` lists it last. So the carrier either does not arrive at all, or, when that launch is the one that starts the service, arrives for **every session the service later serves, across projects**. Neither is a per-launch delivery, and the capture above needed `--standalone` — that requirement is itself the finding. *Two:* OpenCode assembles one system array per session from process-wide state and the `task` tool's child session goes through the same assembly with no gate on its parent, so a `task` subagent receives what the primary agent received; there is no per-agent `instructions` key and no primary-only switch. A quiet worker would get the whole central prefix, which `#SYS-WORKER-EXCLUSION` forbids outright and which `#SYS-HARNESS-DELIVERY`'s row C5 already calls disqualifying — a harness whose subagents inherit the slot must not have `launch` as its default at all. The second blocker is a **source read at 1.19.5** and was not re-measured at 2.2.7, because driving a subagent offline needs a fake provider that emits a tool call; the first blocker alone decides it. **So the shipped behaviour.** Default `read`: `vibe agent opencode` starts OpenCode unchanged, prints the `read` note and one more naming the carrier, the assignment it would have been and why it is not delivered, and the router has the agent read the boot files. A project that declares `delivery = "launch"` gets the **soft launch** of `#SYS-SOFT-LAUNCH` with both blockers and the fix; `vibe prompt flags --harness opencode` refuses there, because it prints and starts nothing. `conflicting_flags` is **empty** for this kind, which is not an omission: vibe passes it no flag under any delivery, so nothing of the user's could be a second one beside ours. **One latent defect was found and fixed by this work.** `HarnessKind::delivery` read `launch` for *every* kind when a node had no `[system_prompt]` table at all, instead of delegating to the table's own per-kind default; harmless while the set held only the two file-slot harnesses, and wrong the moment it did not. It now asks `HarnessTable::default()`, and a test over all three kinds pins it. **What was not done, and why.** The carrier is recorded and measured but **not wired into a delivery**: a carrier that breaks worker exclusion must not be delivered, so building the environment plumbing and the wire member to carry it would have added a surface with no legitimate caller. **Measured live 2026-11-11, on both models the owner named, and at the real size.** OpenCode 2.2.7, Linux. **How the samples were sized is itself a measurement:** OpenCode's fixed overhead came from the offline capture first — a 10,928-byte base system prompt (the project's injected `AGENTS.md` included) plus 14,043 bytes of tool definitions over 12 tools, so **24,971 bytes before any lane** — and at a pessimistic three bytes per token that is roughly 8,300 tokens, which is what tells a 56,000-token model how much lane it can take. **The carrier delivers live at the real size:** on `home/gpt-6.1-sol`, whose provider entry declares a 512,000-token context, the full **204,429-byte** lane handed over by hand — vibe does not deliver it — came back with the last `vibe:lane-end` line quoted **byte-equal**, all four lane canaries present **including the tail** plus the entrypoint's, the template's absent, and **no file read with a tool**: router rule 1 held at 204 KB. On `homelocal/qwen3.8-27b` (56,000 tokens, so a **42,397-byte** lane, the unpadded 2,570-byte one for the other tier) the same answer came back. **The `read` tier — the one that ships — delivers live too:** `vibe agent opencode` passed no flag and `home/gpt-6.1-sol` read `STATIC.md`, `INDEX.md`, `00-core.md` and `90-user.md` in that order, **once each**, reporting every canary and correctly excluding the harness-injected `AGENTS.md` from its read list; asked for the last `vibe:lane-end` line it quoted the managed block's own **format example**, which is the right answer in a tier where no marker is delivered. **One caveat is recorded rather than smoothed over:** that same prompt did *not* make the 27B model boot. It asks only what is in the session's context and which files were opened, and a weaker model answers it literally with zero tool calls; it obeyed rule 4 as soon as the prompt had work in it. Since the stronger model obeyed rule 4 on the one prompt itself, the finding is about model strength and not about the block — and `RESULTS.md` keeps every leg so the two cannot be confused. Reproduction: `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/live/opencode-capture.sh` with `opencode-fake-provider.py`, which calls no model and reaches no network beyond `127.0.0.1`, and drops the `authorization` header before writing a capture. Format record: `SP-FMT-112`; record: `campaigns/sys-prompt-2026-11/live/RESULTS.md` row O1.

p.SYS-REQUEST-ENVELOPE: **Delivered 2026-11-10 (P6) — the request envelope is a document, and a filename chooses no API role.** `vibe prompt capture` lowers `#SYS-CONTINUATION-CACHEABLE`'s prepared materials into the request an API runner sends: the instruction blocks in order (band P, then U, then G), each **placed** in a named instruction role rather than acquiring one by sitting in a file called `SYSTEM.md`; the tool block's position, declared as *ahead* of them because every provider whose cache hierarchy was checked puts tools first; band T, the caller's own, after every instruction block and only in the message role; and the cache-boundary offsets, which are the prepared materials' own and never invented here. Each band's bytes are admitted only against the digest the preparation witnessed, so a file edited in between is a refusal rather than a silently different request. **No double injection**, proved by capturing the actual request at a loopback fake provider and counting: the entrypoint's text, which band P already carries, crosses the wire **exactly once**. **A quiet worker receives no central prefix at all** — a node that has not opted in has no envelope to build, so the prefix is never assembled for it, and the request such a worker does send is asserted on the captured bytes to carry none of the central canaries. **Cache diagnostics are read, never computed**, and that is a type-level guarantee rather than a comment: the diagnostics type has private fields and one constructor, which takes a provider usage record whose own only constructor parses a provider response. A counter the provider did not report is **absent** — never zero, which is a measurement, and never a subtraction, which is why an OpenAI-compatible record (whose prompt total contains the cached part) reports no uncached figure while an Anthropic one (whose `input_tokens` already excludes it) does. **What P6 does not claim**: no cache hit, no TTL, no latency and no saving. The fake-provider capture proves the envelope vibe produced and nothing about a provider's behaviour; `#SYS-CACHE-FACTS` and `#SYS-CACHE-ECONOMICS` keep the rest provider-owned and parametric. It is a separate verb rather than a field on `vibe prompt prepare`, because `prepare`'s own contract is "materials and observations, never a ready-to-send request" and `SP-FMT-011` names a format record of its own. No command in this campaign sends anything. Format record: `SP-FMT-011`.

layering.title: 9. Forward compatibility with the user and override layers

p.SYS-LAYER-ROLE: **Decided 2026-11-10 — this document specifies the `project` layer of PROP-074 `#LAYERED-PREFIX`, and says so in the artifact.** That fact composes one cache-stable prefix from the project layer, the global user project and the project override, in the precedence order of PROP-074 `#OVERRIDE-PRECEDENCE`, with the project layer **first** precisely because it is the most shared and most stable, so that the project's own prefix stays a byte-identical leading part of the composed one. The sidecar therefore carries `layer = "project"` from version 1 and every segment id is layer-qualified from version 1, even though no other layer exists yet. Without a user project or override the composed prefix **is** the project prefix, so the artifact this document specifies is already the whole answer for a project that composes nothing.

p.SYS-LAYER-CONCATENATION: **Decided 2026-11-10 — the four properties that let a later campaign compose layers with no format change here.** **(1) No document-level frame.** The prefix has no opening or closing wrapper, no table of contents and no "this document has N parts" preamble; every separator between *layers* belongs to the composer, and the project layer's bytes end with exactly one LF so a following layer concatenates cleanly (`#SYS-SEGMENT-FRAMING`). **(2) No total digest in the text.** `prefix_sha256` is the project layer's own digest and lives in the sidecar; the composite's digest is the composer's own artifact and never appears inside any layer, so adding a layer cannot change a byte of the project layer. **(3) Layer-qualified ids.** Segment ids and input roles are namespaced by layer, so two layers' sidecars merge without collision and a composer can address one segment of one layer. **(4) A layer-scoped transport contract.** The contract of `#SYS-TRANSPORT-CONTRACT` speaks only for its own layer's supplied sources, so a composer appends each layer's contract instead of regenerating one global one. The composed prefix is personal and must never be committed, which is PROP-074 `#LAYERED-PREFIX-LOCATION`'s rule and that campaign's business — this document's artifacts are committed, and the two are different files in different places.

p.SYS-LAYER-NO-FORMAT-CHANGE: **The prediction this section makes, so it can be falsified.** When the layered-prefix campaign lands, it adds a composer and a personal uncommitted output; it must need **no** change to `vibe-system-prompt/1`, to the segment framing, to the transport-contract recipe or to the three reserved paths. If it does need one, this section was wrong, and the honest record of that is an amendment to this fact rather than a quiet format bump.

p.SYS-OWNER-QUESTIONS: **Open to the owner, each with the default this design takes unless the owner says otherwise.** **(Q1) Is the unconditional INDEX band a cacheable continuation, or baked into the prefix?** Default: **cacheable continuation** (`#SYS-CONTINUATION-CACHEABLE`) — the bytes are cached either way, and baking them would contradict `kind = "static"`'s actual meaning, make freshness much harder to prove, and buy nothing. The alternative, a target-bound fully-frozen snapshot, is a genuinely different contract with a freshness limit, and it would have to be offered as a second profile rather than as this one's default. **(Q2) What override authority do repository, package and user-preference instructions have once they sit in the API instruction role?** Default: the project layer is a trusted application scaffold carrying scoped project policy, user-local preference material never enters the prefix at all, and mandatory external instructions and user-set boundaries are preserved above it; the design does **not** assume the agent-side override semantics carry over unchanged, because the role is not the same role. **(Q3) Portable prefix with gated continuation, or target-bound prefix? ANSWERED by the owner 2026-11-10, and the answer is neither default alone: it is a per-project choice on two separate axes.** See `#SYS-HOST-AND-TARGET`, which governs. `host` (default `"portable"`) decides whether the session's-OS `os:` gates stay in band G or are baked in; `target` (default: every OS) is a new `target:` gate for the product's own platform and is always resolved at build time. The question was posed as one axis and it was two: the proposed default was right for the agent's host and had no answer at all for the product's platform. The original reasoning, kept because it is still why `portable` is the default: OS gates stay in band G and are evaluated against an explicitly supplied session target (`#SYS-SESSION-TARGET`), which is what the committed INDEX design already does; a target-bound prefix is cheaper to send and strictly less reusable, and nothing in this repository needs it today, since every INDEX row here is currently unconditional. **(Q4) How much of the entrypoint must be represented byte-for-byte, versus authored afresh in the template?** Default: **all of it, verbatim**, with the one in-place managed-block substitution of `#SYS-REDIRECT-IN-PLACE` — because no generic prose filter can infer which paragraphs the owner wants dropped, and silently dropping instructions is the worst available failure. The honest cost is `#SYS-ENTRYPOINT-IS-AN-INPUT`: a frequently-edited entrypoint means a frequently-rebuilt prefix, and the remedy is repository hygiene, not an exporter heuristic. **(Q5) Must a measured provider saving exist before the campaign closes?** Default: **no** — the campaign ships the parametric model, the method and the offline envelope proof, and a live cache measurement on named models is a separately authorised follow-up that spends real money and is never run inside the campaign (`#SYS-CACHE-ECONOMICS`). **(Q6) Are the two generated artifacts committed, like `STATIC`/`INDEX`? ANSWERED by the owner 2026-11-10, against this default: they are NOT tracked.** See `#SYS-ARTIFACTS-NOT-TRACKED`, which governs. The default argued that a fresh clone needs no build and that the alternative "would make the prefix unavailable to exactly the zero-dependency case the boot model exists for" — and that was the error: the zero-dependency case is a *session reading files*, which the boot lane serves and the prefix does not. Every consumer of a prefix is a program already invoking `vibe`.

p.SYS-ACCEPTANCE: **The twelve conditions the feature is accepted against**, carried forward from the owner's research proposal and made mechanical where it was prose. (1) The same inputs give a byte-identical `SYSTEM.md` and `SYSTEM.meta.json` in different checkout locations and on Linux, macOS and Windows; a repeated generation neither grows the file nor rewrites it. (2) Neither the template nor either output becomes an ordinary boot input, in legacy discovery or in declared mode; a direct or indirect self-include is refused before any write; a prose mention is not a self-include. (3) Differential scenarios confirm the prefix's static-first order, the continuation's original INDEX order, installed visibility, and gate behaviour for all three operating systems. (4) XML, Markdown, mixed and generated-stream lanes are handled by their existing owners; an authored literal directive or fenced example never becomes an executable import. (5) Root, member and specspace profiles receive nothing outside their selected effective scope while a root's permitted subtree aggregation is preserved, and a quiet worker never receives the central prefix, even temporarily. (7) A missing, unsupported or mutated input, an invalid marker and an output conflict each leave the previous coherent set intact. (8) Home, plan, custody and token sentinel files are never opened and never appear in the output without an explicit separate runtime input; the current task and time never change the prefix.
